Prize share: 1/1

# Marie Curie

## Facts

![Image 3: Nobel Prizes 2026](blob:http://localhost/aef335eb562a1da6957ce25a574b4aa1 [link_27])

Photo from the Nobel Foundation archive.

Marie Curie, née Skłodowska

 Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1911

Born: 7 November 1867, Warsaw, Russian Empire (now Poland)

Died: 4 July 1934, Sallanches, France

Affiliation at the time of the award: Sorbonne University, Paris, France

Prize motivation: “in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element”

Prize share: 1/1

Also awarded: [Nobel Prize in Physics 1903](link_28)

### Life

Marie Skłodowska was born in Warsaw, Poland, to a family of teachers who believed strongly in education. She moved to Paris to continue her studies and there met Pierre Curie, who became both her husband and colleague in the field of radioactivity. The couple later shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics. Marie was widowed in 1906, but continued the couple's work and went on to become the first person ever to be awarded two Nobel Prizes. During World War I, Curie organized mobile X-ray teams. The Curies' daughter, Irene, was also jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alongside her husband, Frederic Joliot

### Work

After Marie Skłodowska Curie and Pierre Curie first discovered the radioactive elements polonium and radium, Marie continued to investigate their properties. In 1910 she successfully produced radium as a pure metal, which proved the new element's existence beyond a doubt. She also documented the properties of the radioactive elements and their compounds. Radioactive compounds became important as sources of radiation in both scientific experiments and in the field of medicine, where they are used to treat tumors.

# Marie Curie

## Facts

![Image 3: Nobel Prizes 2026](blob:http://localhost/aef335eb562a1da6957ce25a574b4aa1 [link_27])

Photo from the Nobel Foundation archive.

Marie Curie, née Skłodowska

 Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1911

Born: 7 November 1867, Warsaw, Russian Empire (now Poland)

Died: 4 July 1934, Sallanches, France

Affiliation at the time of the award: Sorbonne University, Paris, France

Prize motivation: “in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element”

Prize share: 1/1

Also awarded: [Nobel Prize in Physics 1903](link_28)

### Life

Marie Skłodowska was born in Warsaw, Poland, to a family of teachers who believed strongly in education. She moved to Paris to continue her studies and there met Pierre Curie, who became both her husband and colleague in the field of radioactivity. The couple later shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics. Marie was widowed in 1906, but continued the couple's work and went on to become the first person ever to be awarded two Nobel Prizes. During World War I, Curie organized mobile X-ray teams. The Curies' daughter, Irene, was also jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alongside her husband, Frederic Joliot

### Work

After Marie Skłodowska Curie and Pierre Curie first discovered the radioactive elements polonium and radium, Marie continued to investigate their properties. In 1910 she successfully produced radium as a pure metal, which proved the new element's existence beyond a doubt. She also documented the properties of the radioactive elements and their compounds. Radioactive compounds became important as sources of radiation in both scientific experiments and in the field of medicine, where they are used to treat tumors.

# All Nobel Prizes

Between 1901 and 2026, the Nobel Prizes and the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel were awarded 639 times to 1,036 people and organisations. With some receiving the Nobel Prize more than once, this makes a total of 1,000 individuals and 28 organisations. Below, you can view the full list of Nobel Prizes and Nobel Prize laureates.

## Find all prizes in | [physics](link_16) | [chemistry](link_17) | [physiology or medicine](link_18) | [literature](link_19) | [peace](link_20) | [economic sciences](link_21) | [all categories](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/lists/all-nobel-prizes/)

* * *

## 2026

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2026](link_22)

[Francis Halzen](link_23)

> “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”

### [Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2026](link_24)

[Henri B. Kagan](link_25) and [Kenso Soai](link_26)

> “for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”

### [Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2026](link_27)

[Karl Deisseroth](link_28), [Peter Hegemann](link_29) and [Georg Nagel](link_30)

> “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”

### [Nobel Prize in Literature 2026](link_31)

[Anne Carson](link_32)

> “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”

### [Nobel Peace Prize 2026](link_33)

[Navi Pillay](link_34)

> “for her efforts to promote peace and international law”

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2026](link_35)

[Robert E. Hall](link_36) and [Michael Woodford](link_37)

> “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”

## 2025

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2025](link_38)

[John Clarke](link_39), [Michel H. Devoret](link_40) and [John M. Martinis](link_41)

> “for the discovery of macroscopic quantum mechanical tunnelling and energy quantisation in an electric circuit”

### [Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2025](link_42)

[Susumu Kitagawa](link_43), [Richard Robson](link_44) and [Omar M. Yaghi](link_45)

> “for the development of metal–organic frameworks”

### [Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2025](link_46)

[Mary E. Brunkow](link_47), [Fred Ramsdell](link_48) and [Shimon Sakaguchi](link_49)

> “for their discoveries concerning peripheral immune tolerance”

### [Nobel Prize in Literature 2025](link_50)

[László Krasznahorkai](link_51)

> “for his compelling and visionary oeuvre that, in the midst of apocalyptic terror, reaffirms the power of art”

### [Nobel Peace Prize 2025](link_52)

[Maria Corina Machado](link_53)

> “for her tireless work promoting democratic rights for the people of Venezuela and for her struggle to achieve a just and peaceful transition from dictatorship to democracy”

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2025](link_54)

> “for having explained innovation-driven economic growth”

[Joel Mokyr](link_55)

> “for having identified the prerequisites for sustained growth through technological progress”

[Philippe Aghion](link_56) and [Peter Howitt](link_57)

> “for the theory of sustained growth through creative destruction”

## 2024

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2024](link_58)

[John J. Hopfield](link_59) and [Geoffrey Hinton](link_60)

> “for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks”

### [Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2024](link_61)

[David Baker](link_62)

> “for computational protein design”

[Demis Hassabis](link_63) and [John Jumper](link_64)

> “for protein structure prediction”

### [Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2024](link_65)

[Victor Ambros](link_66) and [Gary Ruvkun](link_67)

> “for the discovery of microRNA and its role in post-transcriptional gene regulation”

### [Nobel Prize in Literature 2024](link_68)

[Han Kang](link_69)

> “for her intense poetic prose that confronts historical traumas and exposes the fragility of human life”

### [Nobel Peace Prize 2024](link_70)

[Nihon Hidankyo](link_71)

> “for its efforts to achieve a world free of nuclear weapons and for demonstrating through witness testimony that nuclear weapons must never be used again”

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2024](link_72)

[Daron Acemoglu](link_73), [Simon Johnson](link_74) and [James A. Robinson](link_75)

> “for studies of how institutions are formed and affect prosperity”

## 2023

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2023](link_76)

[Pierre Agostini](link_77), [Ferenc Krausz](link_78) and [Anne L’Huillier](link_79)

> “for experimental methods that generate attosecond pulses of light for the study of electron dynamics in matter”

### [Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2023](link_80)

[Moungi Bawendi](link_81), [Louis Brus](link_82) and [Aleksey Yekimov](link_83)

> “for the discovery and synthesis of quantum dots”

### [Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2023](link_84)

[Katalin Karikó](link_85) and [Drew Weissman](link_86)

> “for their discoveries concerning nucleoside base modifications that enabled the development of effective mRNA vaccines against COVID-19”

### [Nobel Prize in Literature 2023](link_87)

[Jon Fosse](link_88)

> “for his innovative plays and prose which give voice to the unsayable”

### [Nobel Peace Prize 2023](link_89)

[Narges Mohammadi](link_90)

> “for her fight against the oppression of women in Iran and her fight to promote human rights and freedom for all”

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2023](link_91)

[Claudia Goldin](link_92)

> “for having advanced our understanding of women’s labour market outcomes”

## 2022

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2022](link_93)

[Alain Aspect](link_94), [John Clauser](link_95) and [Anton Zeilinger](link_96)

> “for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell inequalities and pioneering quantum information science”

### [Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2022](link_97)

[Carolyn Bertozzi](link_98), [Morten Meldal](link_99) and [K. Barry Sharpless](link_100)

> “for the development of click chemistry and bioorthogonal chemistry”

### [Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2022](link_101)

[Svante Pääbo](link_102)

> “for his discoveries concerning the genomes of extinct hominins and human evolution”

### [Nobel Prize in Literature 2022](link_103)

[Annie Ernaux](link_104)

> “for the courage and clinical acuity with which she uncovers the roots, estrangements and collective restraints of personal memory”

### [Nobel Peace Prize 2022](link_105)

[Ales Bialiatski](link_106), [Memorial](link_107) and [Center for Civil Liberties](link_108)

> “The Peace Prize laureates represent civil society in their home countries. They have for many years promoted the right to criticise power and protect the fundamental rights of citizens. They have made an outstanding effort to document war crimes, human right abuses and the abuse of power. Together they demonstrate the significance of civil society for peace and democracy”

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2022](link_109)

[Ben Bernanke](link_110), [Douglas Diamond](link_111) and [Philip Dybvig](link_112)

> “for research on banks and financial crises”

## 2021

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2021](link_113)

> “for groundbreaking contributions to our understanding of complex physical systems”

[Syukuro Manabe](link_114) and [Klaus Hasselmann](link_115)

> “for the physical modelling of Earth’s climate, quantifying variability and reliably predicting global warming”

[Giorgio Parisi](link_116)

> “for the discovery of the interplay of disorder and fluctuations in physical systems from atomic to planetary scales”

### [Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2021](link_117)

[Benjamin List](link_118) and [David W.C. MacMillan](link_119)

> “for the development of asymmetric organocatalysis”

### [Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2021](link_120)

[David Julius](link_121) and [Ardem Patapoutian](link_122)

> “for their discoveries of receptors for temperature and touch”

### [Nobel Prize in Literature 2021](link_123)

[Abdulrazak Gurnah](link_124)

> “for his uncompromising and compassionate penetration of the effects of colonialism and the fate of the refugee in the gulf between cultures and continents”

### [Nobel Peace Prize 2021](link_125)

## Facts
![Image 3: Nobel Prizes 2026](blob:http://localhost/aef335eb562a1da6957ce25a574b4aa1)
Photo from the Nobel Foundation archive.
Marie Curie, née Skłodowska
Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1911
Born: 7 November 1867, Warsaw, Russian Empire (now Poland)
Died: 4 July 1934, Sallanches, France
Affiliation at the time of the award: Sorbonne University, Paris, France
Prize motivation: “in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element”
Prize share: 1/1
Also awarded: [Nobel Prize in Physics 1903](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1903/summary/)

# Marie Curie
## Facts
### Life
Marie Skłodowska was born in Warsaw, Poland, to a family of teachers who believed strongly in education. She moved to Paris to continue her studies and there met Pierre Curie, who became both her husband and colleague in the field of radioactivity. The couple later shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics. Marie was widowed in 1906, but continued the couple's work and went on to become the first person ever to be awarded two Nobel Prizes. During World War I, Curie organized mobile X-ray teams. The Curies' daughter, Irene, was also jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alongside her husband, Frederic Joliot

# Marie Curie
## Facts
### Work
After Marie Skłodowska Curie and Pierre Curie first discovered the radioactive elements polonium and radium, Marie continued to investigate their properties. In 1910 she successfully produced radium as a pure metal, which proved the new element's existence beyond a doubt. She also documented the properties of the radioactive elements and their compounds. Radioactive compounds became important as sources of radiation in both scientific experiments and in the field of medicine, where they are used to treat tumors.

Marie Curie, née Skłodowska
Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1911
Born: 7 November 1867, Warsaw, Russian Empire (now Poland)

Prize share: 1/1

# Marie Curie
## Facts
### Life
Marie Skłodowska was born in Warsaw, Poland, to a family of teachers who believed strongly in education. She moved to Paris to continue her studies and there met Pierre Curie, who became both her husband and colleague in the field of radioactivity. The couple later shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics. Marie was widowed in 1906, but continued the couple's work and went on to become the first person ever to be awarded two Nobel Prizes. During World War I, Curie organized mobile X-ray teams. The Curies' daughter, Irene, was also jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alongside her husband, Frederic Joliot

# Marie Curie
## Facts
### Work
After Marie Skłodowska Curie and Pierre Curie first discovered the radioactive elements polonium and radium, Marie continued to investigate their properties. In 1910 she successfully produced radium as a pure metal, which proved the new element's existence beyond a doubt. She also documented the properties of the radioactive elements and their compounds. Radioactive compounds became important as sources of radiation in both scientific experiments and in the field of medicine, where they are used to treat tumors.

Marie Curie, née Skłodowska
Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1911
Born: 7 November 1867, Warsaw, Russian Empire (now Poland)
Died: 4 July 1934, Sallanches, France
Affiliation at the time of the award: Sorbonne University, Paris, France
Prize motivation: “in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element”
Prize share: 1/1
Also awarded: [Nobel Prize in Physics 1903](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1903/summary/)

# Marie Curie
## Facts
### Life
Marie Skłodowska was born in Warsaw, Poland, to a family of teachers who believed strongly in education. She moved to Paris to continue her studies and there met Pierre Curie, who became both her husband and colleague in the field of radioactivity. The couple later shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics. Marie was widowed in 1906, but continued the couple's work and went on to become the first person ever to be awarded two Nobel Prizes. During World War I, Curie organized mobile X-ray teams. The Curies' daughter, Irene, was also jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alongside her husband, Frederic Joliot

# Marie Curie
## Facts
### Work
After Marie Skłodowska Curie and Pierre Curie first discovered the radioactive elements polonium and radium, Marie continued to investigate their properties. In 1910 she successfully produced radium as a pure metal, which proved the new element's existence beyond a doubt. She also documented the properties of the radioactive elements and their compounds. Radioactive compounds became important as sources of radiation in both scientific experiments and in the field of medicine, where they are used to treat tumors.

# Marie Curie
## Facts
### Life
Marie Skłodowska was born in Warsaw, Poland, to a family of teachers who believed strongly in education. She moved to Paris to continue her studies and there met Pierre Curie, who became both her husband and colleague in the field of radioactivity. The couple later shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics. Marie was widowed in 1906, but continued the couple's work and went on to become the first person ever to be awarded two Nobel Prizes. During World War I, Curie organized mobile X-ray teams. The Curies' daughter, Irene, was also jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alongside her husband, Frederic Joliot

## Facts
### Work
After Marie Skłodowska Curie and Pierre Curie first discovered the radioactive elements polonium and radium, Marie continued to investigate their properties. In 1910 she successfully produced radium as a pure metal, which proved the new element's existence beyond a doubt. She also documented the properties of the radioactive elements and their compounds. Radioactive compounds became important as sources of radiation in both scientific experiments and in the field of medicine, where they are used to treat tumors.

# Marie Curie

## Facts

![Image 3: Nobel Prizes 2026](blob:http://localhost/aef335eb562a1da6957ce25a574b4aa1 [link_27])

Photo from the Nobel Foundation archive.

Marie Curie, née Skłodowska

 Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1911

Born: 7 November 1867, Warsaw, Russian Empire (now Poland)

Died: 4 July 1934, Sallanches, France

Affiliation at the time of the award: Sorbonne University, Paris, France

Prize motivation: “in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element”

Prize share: 1/1

Also awarded: [Nobel Prize in Physics 1903](link_28)

### Life

Marie Skłodowska was born in Warsaw, Poland, to a family of teachers who believed strongly in education. She moved to Paris to continue her studies and there met Pierre Curie, who became both her husband and colleague in the field of radioactivity. The couple later shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics. Marie was widowed in 1906, but continued the couple's work and went on to become the first person ever to be awarded two Nobel Prizes. During World War I, Curie organized mobile X-ray teams. The Curies' daughter, Irene, was also jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alongside her husband, Frederic Joliot

### Work

After Marie Skłodowska Curie and Pierre Curie first discovered the radioactive elements polonium and radium, Marie continued to investigate their properties. In 1910 she successfully produced radium as a pure metal, which proved the new element's existence beyond a doubt. She also documented the properties of the radioactive elements and their compounds. Radioactive compounds became important as sources of radiation in both scientific experiments and in the field of medicine, where they are used to treat tumors.

# Marie Curie
## Facts
### Life
Marie Skłodowska was born in Warsaw, Poland, to a family of teachers who believed strongly in education. She moved to Paris to continue her studies and there met Pierre Curie, who became both her husband and colleague in the field of radioactivity. The couple later shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics. Marie was widowed in 1906, but continued the couple's work and went on to become the first person ever to be awarded two Nobel Prizes. During World War I, Curie organized mobile X-ray teams. The Curies' daughter, Irene, was also jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alongside her husband, Frederic Joliot

Original direct_answer chunk 6:
# Marie Curie
## Facts
### Work
After Marie Skłodowska Curie and Pierre Curie first discovered the radioactive elements polonium and radium, Marie continued to investigate their properties. In 1910 she successfully produced radium as a pure metal, which proved the new element's existence beyond a doubt. She also documented the properties of the radioactive elements and their compounds. Radioactive compounds became important as sources of radiation in both scientific experiments and in the field of medicine, where they are used to treat tumors.

# Marie Curie
## Facts
### Life
Marie Skłodowska was born in Warsaw, Poland, to a family of teachers who believed strongly in education. She moved to Paris to continue her studies and there met Pierre Curie, who became both her husband and colleague in the field of radioactivity. The couple later shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics. Marie was widowed in 1906, but continued the couple's work and went on to become the first person ever to be awarded two Nobel Prizes. During World War I, Curie organized mobile X-ray teams. The Curies' daughter, Irene, was also jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alongside her husband, Frederic Joliot

Original direct_answer chunk 6:
# Marie Curie
## Facts
### Work
After Marie Skłodowska Curie and Pierre Curie first discovered the radioactive elements polonium and radium, Marie continued to investigate their properties. In 1910 she successfully produced radium as a pure metal, which proved the new element's existence beyond a doubt. She also documented the properties of the radioactive elements and their compounds. Radioactive compounds became important as sources of radiation in both scientific experiments and in the field of medicine, where they are used to treat tumors.

# All Nobel Prizes
Between 1901 and 2026, the Nobel Prizes and the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel were awarded 639 times to 1,036 people and organisations. With some receiving the Nobel Prize more than once, this makes a total of 1,000 individuals and 28 organisations. Below, you can view the full list of Nobel Prizes and Nobel Prize laureates.

# Marie Curie
## Facts
### Life
Marie Skłodowska was born in Warsaw, Poland, to a family of teachers who believed strongly in education. She moved to Paris to continue her studies and there met Pierre Curie, who became both her husband and colleague in the field of radioactivity. The couple later shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics. Marie was widowed in 1906, but continued the couple's work and went on to become the first person ever to be awarded two Nobel Prizes. During World War I, Curie organized mobile X-ray teams. The Curies' daughter, Irene, was also jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alongside her husband, Frederic Joliot

# Marie Curie
## Facts
### Work
After Marie Skłodowska Curie and Pierre Curie first discovered the radioactive elements polonium and radium, Marie continued to investigate their properties. In 1910 she successfully produced radium as a pure metal, which proved the new element's existence beyond a doubt. She also documented the properties of the radioactive elements and their compounds. Radioactive compounds became important as sources of radiation in both scientific experiments and in the field of medicine, where they are used to treat tumors.
